transcript.content: hey, i'm berry. tell me your dream, however it comes back to you.
I was on a night bus with my younger brother, going home in the rain. It was almost empty.
a night bus, rain, almost no one on it. that sounds quiet in a particular way. what happened?
Just the driver and an old woman knitting at the back. My brother was holding a paper lantern with a candle inside it.
a paper lantern with a real candle in it, on a bus in the rain. that seems so fragile. why was he holding it?
I don't know why. He just had it.
fair enough. dreams don't always explain things like that. so you're on the bus, he's holding the lantern, the old woman's knitting. what happened next?
I looked out the window and the street lights were melting into long orange ribbons.
melting into ribbons... that sounds almost hypnotic. how did the light look from inside the bus, with all that rain on the windows?
It was blurry, like the rain made everything smear together. The orange just stretched across the glass.
so the whole window was just orange smeared across it. did it make the inside of the bus feel different at all?
Not really, it was still dark inside except for the candle in the lantern.
the candle was the only real light in there, everything else dark and smeared. that must have made the lantern feel like the center of things.
Yeah, kind of. It glowed warm next to my brother.
that's a warm image, in the middle of all that rain and dark. and you, in that moment on the bus... were you there as yourself, sitting next to him?
I think I was sitting beside him, but the next thing I remember is I was standing in my grandmother's kitchen.
oh, that's a jump. from the bus to your grandmother's kitchen just like that. what was the kitchen like, when you found yourself standing there?
It was morning. My grandmother was at the stove making tea. Her hair was completely white.
morning, so bright compared to the bus. and your grandmother there at the stove. what did the kitchen look like?
It was warm and clean. I remember the stove and the smell of tea.
warm and clean, with that smell of tea. it sounds like a peaceful place. did she say anything to you?
Not yet. But my brother was there too, still holding the lantern, only now it was glowing blue.
the lantern turned blue. even in your grandmother's sunny kitchen, the light from it changed. did anything else feel different in the kitchen because of that?
It felt strange, because it didn't fit the morning. And then I saw neighbours squeezed into the doorway watching us.
neighbours squeezed into the doorway, watching. that's such a sudden crowd in a place that felt just for family. how did they seem?
Quiet. Maybe eight or ten of them, just standing and watching.
so still and quiet, all of them. and you were there, the blue lantern, your grandmother making tea, all these watching faces. what did it feel like to be looked at like that?
It felt like they were waiting for something, but I didn't know what.
right, like the air was holding its breath. did anything happen with the lantern, or with your brother, with them all standing there?
Then the kitchen table turned into a small wooden boat. My grandmother told me to get in.
the table just became a boat. and your grandmother told you to get in, not your brother. what did the boat look like?
Small, made of wood. Like a rowboat, but old. Nothing fancy.
an old wooden rowboat in the middle of the kitchen. it must have been strange to step into something like that indoors. did you get in?
Yes, I got in. Then it floated out the kitchen door and back onto the street where the bus had been.
the street where the bus had been, now you're floating in a boat. was it still raining there?
I don't remember rain. The street had turned into a river.

so you were on a night bus with your younger brother, going home in the rain. almost empty, just the driver and an old woman knitting at the back. your brother was holding a paper lantern with a candle inside, warm glow next to him. the street lights outside were melting into long orange ribbons, blurry with rain smeared across the glass, everything dark inside except that candle. then you were standing in your grandmother's kitchen, morning, warm and clean, her hair white, making tea. your brother was there, the lantern now glowing blue. neighbours squeezed into the doorway, eight or ten of them, quiet, watching, waiting for something. then the kitchen table turned into an old wooden rowboat, and your grandmother told you to get in. you did, and it floated out the door back onto the street, but no rain now, the street had turned into a river.

did i get that right? and is that where the dream ended, or was there more after?
That's right. My brother waved at me from the bank, still holding the blue lantern. Then I woke up.

so you ended up on the river, and he stayed on the bank with the lantern, waving. that final image, him there with the blue light while you drifted... that's what would linger for me, if it were my dream. what was it like, that last moment?
It felt sad but calm. Like I was leaving him behind.
was there any object from the dream that felt especially yours, something that mattered in a way you can't quite name? maybe the lantern, or the boat, or something smaller?
The lantern felt like the center of everything. Even when it turned blue it still did.

your brother waved at you from the bank, still holding the blue lantern, and then you woke up.

did i get that right? and that was the end of the dream?
Yes, that's right. That was the end.
i think i have a good sense of your dream now. would you like to see it drawn?
Yes, I would.

of course.

which feels closest to how your dream looked? or would you describe your own way?
A bit soft and glowing, especially the lantern light. Not too sharp.

okay, soft and glowing, especially the lantern light. not too sharp. i'll start with the street turned river.

for the street turned river, i'm picturing banks along the side, water flowing where the street used to be. and the light... i'd guess it's overcast or evening, but not raining. those are my guesses, though. does anything feel different, or should i just go with that?
Go with that. That could be how it looked.

okay, i'm sketching the street turned river, your younger brother, the bus driver, the old woman, your grandmother, the night bus, your grandmother's kitchen, the paper lantern, and the rowboat now — it'll appear on the right. just that for now.

and since you're in it too, i'd love to draw you as well. would you like to be drawn as you are — you can tell me a little about yourself — or however i imagine you?
You can imagine me.
got it. i'm sketching you now — everything's being drawn and will show up on the right over the next minute or two. once it's there, you can tell me if anything looks off.
Alright.
take your time. i'm here.
Well, I don't see anything yet, but take your time.

i'm sorry — i wasn't able to draw it. something's gone wrong on my side, and no moment from your dream actually came through. that's not the way it should have gone, and i'm sorry.

thank you for sharing it with me, though. the lantern, the river, your brother on the bank — it stays with me.

moments.action: On a night bus, the dreamer and their younger brother sit together; the brother holds a paper lantern with a candle inside, glowing warm. The bus is almost empty, with only the driver and an old woman knitting at the back.
Through the bus window, street lights melt into long orange ribbons, smeared across the rain-blurred glass.
In the grandmother's kitchen in the morning, the grandmother stands at the stove making tea; her hair is completely white. The dreamer stands in the kitchen.
The dreamer's younger brother is also in the kitchen, still holding the paper lantern, but now the lantern glows blue. The dreamer notices the strangeness of the blue light in the sunny morning.
Neighbours, eight or ten of them, are squeezed into the doorway of the kitchen, quiet, watching the dreamer and their brother and grandmother. They seem to be waiting for something.
The kitchen table turns into a small wooden rowboat. The grandmother tells the dreamer to get in.
The dreamer gets into the boat. It floats out the kitchen door and onto the street, which has turned into a river.
The dreamer is in the boat on the river. The younger brother stands on the bank, still holding the blue lantern, waving at the dreamer. The dreamer drifts away.
